books.section: Unit 5: Toward the Civil War and Reconstruction (1844–1877)

primary_sources: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom's Cabin, vol. 1 (1852)

stimulus.source_note: Harriet Beecher Stowe, Uncle Tom's Cabin; or, Life Among the Lowly, vol. 1, title page (Boston: John P. Jewett & Company, 1852). Public domain.
stimulus.text: The title page of the first book edition of Uncle Tom's Cabin, published in Boston in 1852, reads “UNCLE TOM'S CABIN; OR, LIFE AMONG THE LOWLY. BY HARRIET BEECHER STOWE.” Below the title, an engraving shows a woman standing in the doorway of a log cabin, with children and a man carrying an axe nearby. The page also states “VOL. I.” and “TENTH THOUSAND,” meaning ten thousand copies had already been printed.

rationales.A: The novel attacks slavery's cruelty; it does not defend the act that returned runaways.
rationales.B: Background from the books: Stowe wrote the novel after the Fugitive Slave Act of 1850, and its scenes of enslaved families torn apart made slavery vivid for readers who had never seen a plantation.
rationales.C: The novel opposes slavery's expansion; it never argues for spreading slavery westward.
rationales.D: Background from the books: Stowe was a Northerner from a Connecticut antislavery family, writing in Ohio and Maine — not a Southern planter.
rationales.general:
1. Picture the cabin on the title page: a woman at the door, children at her feet, a family at home.
2. Ask what that picture does to a reader: it turns slavery from an argument into a family that can be torn apart.
3. Background from the books: the novel came two years after the Fugitive Slave Act, when Northerners were meeting the slavery question on their own streets.
Remember: a story can do what a speech cannot — make strangers feel what an argument only describes.
